cells.tense: You are at the end of something and you are the one holding the pen.
cells.ask: Pick one finished thing and say out loud that it is done. Then leave it alone for the rest of the day and start nothing new to replace it.
cells.core:
You end things well. Not by holding on and not by walking away early — you finish, you look at what you made, and then you let it go without flinching. That's a harder combination than it sounds, and it's what makes the next thing possible.
What's here now is that the ending isn't a loss for you. Something is wrapping up and you can feel the plain rightness of that, the way you can feel a door close. The care you've been putting into it turns into care for whatever comes after, and it doesn't drain you to keep caring. You're free to feed that next thing now, or not. It's an invitation, not a debt.
cells.sheetLine: You finish things and you let them go, and that's the skill.
cells.verb: finishing what you started and letting the finished thing go
cells.place: the point where a thing completed becomes the ground for what comes next

cells.tense: You are standing at a finish line that hasn't been reached yet, gripping.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are treating as finished that is still running. Put it down for one day and let it run without you.
cells.core:
You're ending things ahead of time. Somewhere in front of you is the moment everything will be settled — done, signed, closed — and you're already living there, trying to force the last pages to write themselves. So you release things before they're complete, or you push a completion that isn't yours to push.
The rehearsing is the tell. When you catch yourself planning the aftermath of something that hasn't happened, that's the finishing instinct running ahead of what's actually finished. The instinct itself is real and it's good; it just has no finish line to stand on yet, so it's gripping whatever is nearest. Slow the release down to the pace of what's actually ending. It doesn't need a push from you.
cells.sheetLine: You're closing things that are still open.
cells.verb: finishing what you started and letting the finished thing go

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed and you have not stepped through.
cells.ask: Take one task you have been re-opening and build it a container — a fixed hour, a set stopping point. Work inside it and stop when the hour ends.
cells.core:
The endings don't stay ended. You finish something, and then you're back at the doorstep, reworking it, unable to set it down. The completion isn't underneath you; you're standing in front of it with the thing still open in your hands.
More effort at the old door won't do it. A place to build from is what's needed here. You do better with something solid underfoot — a routine, a structure, a container you can hold — and right now there isn't one, so the old thing keeps pulling you back. Give yourself a small structure to work inside, one that holds on its own without you gripping it. That steadiness is where your finishing power comes back from.
cells.sheetLine: You keep returning to a door you already closed.

cells.tense: You are done with something and calling the ending the thing's own doing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you finished this year and say plainly that you finished it. Write it down in your own words before you move on.
cells.core:
You've been ending things on purpose for a while now. You choose where a thing finishes, you let go of what's finished, and you don't look back — but you describe it like it just happened, like the ending was the situation's idea and not yours.
That move is why the endings don't feel like yours. You're tending whatever comes next with the same patience you brought to the last thing, and it's working. When you decide a thing is done, that's you deciding. It's quiet and it's regular and it's all yours, and it would hold more if you claimed it. Not as a story about you, just as a fact. You're the one who decides when a thing is done here.
cells.sheetLine: You choose when things end. You call it just how it went.
